title: The translator's margin
bodyMd:
Original humanities exposition.

When a small press prepared a new translation of a nineteenth-century travel diary, the translator encountered a word that could mean either a broad public square or a market held within one. The diary's author described entering it at dawn, hearing traders call, and then crossing it again at dusk after the stalls had vanished. An earlier translation used "market" in both places.

The new translator chose "square." The choice preserved the continuity of the physical setting: a reader could imagine the same space changing as the day passed. It also lost something. The first appearance of the word in the original could evoke the gathering of traders as readily as the paved location beneath them. English offered no single everyday word carrying precisely the same combination.

Rather than conceal this decision, the translator added a brief note explaining the ambiguity. The editor worried that notes would interrupt the diary's pace. They agreed to place the note at the back, with a small reference mark in the text. Readers could follow the journey uninterrupted or pause to examine the choice.

The case illustrates a difficulty broader than deciding which dictionary entry is correct. Translation requires distributing meaning across the main text and the apparatus around it. A note cannot restore every association of the source word, but it can make a consequential decision available for scrutiny. Fluency remains a goal; it need not require pretending that no decisions were made.
